query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an in‐situ, pulsed-laser remelting pass immediately after the deposition of each layer will simultaneously refine the microstructure, homogenize residual stresses, and self-level the deposited geometry, thereby improving dimensional precision, mechanical integrity, and reducing fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited HEA components produced by SLM that exhibit thermal-gradient-induced defects such as cracks, irregular layer geometry, and residual stress-related microstructural inhomogeneities.
generation.intervention: A single-step in-situ pulsed-laser remelting process applied immediately after each deposited layer.
generation.conditions: Conducted in a standard SLM setup for HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn or similar systems) in an inert atmosphere; pulsed remelting to be executed at a lower energy density and a modulated scanning speed optimized to avoid high back reflections, with parameters adjusted in real time based on melt pool feedback.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in thermal gradients and residual stresses leading to grain refinement and improved layer-bed conformity.
generation.mechanism: The brief, controlled remelting pass re-melts only the surface of the deposited layer, which promotes microstructural homogenization and partial reflow of material to counteract surface irregularities, while the pulsed operation minimizes excessive energy input. This reduces the formation of microcracks and porosities caused by rapid cooling, thus enhancing both dimensional precision and overall mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with standard SLM parts, the intervention should yield components with reduced defect density (fewer cracks and porosities), improved dimensional fidelity (closer adherence to design geometry), and enhanced mechanical properties (increased tensile strength and ductility due to a more uniform and refined grain structure).
generation.baseline: HEA components produced via conventional SLM using optimized process parameters but without any in-situ remelting post-treatment, which typically exhibit residual defects and dimensional deviations due to rapid solidification.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for HEAs processed by SLM under conditions where thermal gradients are significant; however, the precise magnitude of improvements may vary with alloy composition and specific SLM parameters.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from laser remelting benefits on Al0.65CoCrFeNi (PMC9919236) and scanning speed effects in CoCrNi MEA (PMC10772231), while addressing the challenge of technical issues (such as high back reflections) noted in the DED studies of CrNbTiZr (PMC12348559). The extrapolation to a pulsed in-situ remelting process in SLM for defect mitigation in HEAs is novel and untested, thus carrying uncertainty regarding optimal pulse parameters and integration with existing scanning strategies.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of identical HEA components by SLM: one group incorporating the proposed in-situ pulsed-laser remelting after each layer, and a control group using standard SLM parameters with no remelting. Ensure all other processing variables are held constant. Use statistical sampling to ensure reproducibility.
measurements: Dimensional analysis of components (using high-precision metrology) to quantify deviations from the designed geometry.
Microstructural evaluation via SEM and X-ray CT to assess defect density (cracks, porosities) and grain refinement.
Mechanical testing (tensile and fatigue tests) to determine improvements in strength, ductility, and resistance to failure.
Residual stress measurements (e.g., using X-ray diffraction) to quantify stress homogenization.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA components produced with the in-situ pulsed-laser remelting do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy (e.g., reduced geometric deviation), a lower defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and ductility) compared to the control group, or if new processing challenges emerge that negate the benefits, then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Medium entropy alloy (MEA) is a hot spot in the field of material research in recent years. At present, the most widely used processing method of MEAs is “casting-rolling-heat treatment”, and the preparation of CoCrNi MEA by laser additive manufacturing (LAM) is still in primary stage. In this study, CoCrNi MEAs were fabricated with different scanning speeds by laser additive manufacturing, and the influence of scanning speed on its mechanical properties was investigated. The results show that higher scanning speed can significantly improve the mechanical properties of CoCrNi MEA. Compared with the low-speed laser additive manufacturing (LSLAM) MEA, the tensile strength of high-speed laser additive manufacturing (HSLAM) MEA is increased by 5.6 % and the fracture strain is increased by 60 %, which is mainly due to the entanglement of 1/6<112> and 1/2<110> dislocations and the defect structure at the grain boundary. LAM is a promising technology that can promote the development and application of MEAs in industry.

The present study demonstrates that a strategic combination of deposition-parameters optimization and thermal management enables the fabrication of a crack-free bulk CrNbTiZr RCCA via L-DED using elemental powders. This represents a significant advancement, as prior efforts involving DED of similar systems have typically been limited to thin-wall geometries and have often suffered from severe cracking, substantial residual porosity, or incomplete fusion [,,,,,,]. Our results indicate that insulating the build platform and minimizing the dwell time between the layers elevates the overall temperature of the sample, effectively preventing the formation of macrocracks. It can be attributed to the fact that the deposition on insulated substrate reduces temperature gradients created at the edge of the melt pool which in turn decreases the strain concentrations and suppresses the formation of cracks. In contrast, samples deposited on the thermally conductive platform exhibited pronounced cracking. A laser-induced pre-heating temperature of approximately 500 °C was determined to be adequate to achieve this effect.

The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential. The microstructure of the remelted layer was refined from coarse dendritic to submicron-scale basket weave compared with the as-cast substrate, resulting in a 1.8-time increase in Vickers microhardness. The nanoindentation tests indicated that the nanohardness of the remelted layer was higher than that of each phase in the substrate. Meanwhile, the remelted layer retained considerable plasticity, as evidenced by its high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and strain hardening exponent (0.302). Additionally, adhesive wear prevailed on the substrate, while only abrasive wear features were observed on the remelted layer. Accordingly, the average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted layer were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the substrate. Our findings explored an industrialized method to enhance the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA and also provided some helpful references for its laser additive manufacturing.
